In statistics, '''kernel-independent component analysis (kernel ICA)''' is an efficient algorithm for [[independent component analysis]] which estimates source components by optimizing a ''generalized variance'' contrast function, which is based on representations in a [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]].<ref name = "Bach Jordan JMLR 2003">{{Cite journal | last1 = Bach | first1 = Francis R. | last2 = Jordan | first2 = Michael I. | doi = 10.1162/153244303768966085 | title = Kernel independent component analysis | journal = The Journal of Machine Learning Research | volume = 3 | pages = 1–48 | year = 2003 | url = https://www.di.ens.fr/~fbach/kernelICA-jmlr.pdf}}</ref><ref name = "Bach Jordan ICASSP 2003">{{Cite book | last1 = Bach | first1 = Francis R. | last2 = Jordan | first2 = Michael I. | title = 2003 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, 2003. Proceedings. (ICASSP '03) | chapter = Kernel independent component analysis | doi = 10.1109/icassp.2003.1202783 | volume = 4 | pages = IV-876-9 | year = 2003 | url = https://www.di.ens.fr/~fbach/kernelICA-icassp03.pdf| isbn = 978-0-7803-7663-2 | s2cid = 7691428 }}</ref> Those contrast functions use the notion of [[mutual information]] as a [[Independent component analysis#Defining component independence|measure]] of [[Independence (probability theory)|statistical independence]].

==Main idea==
Kernel ICA is based on the idea that correlations between two random variables  can be represented in a [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space|reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS)]], denoted by <math>\mathcal{F}</math>, associated with a feature map <math>L_x: \mathcal{F} \mapsto \mathbb{R} </math> defined for a fixed <math>x \in \mathbb{R}</math>. The <math>\mathcal{F}</math>-correlation  between two random variables <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> is defined as

: <math> \rho_{\mathcal{F}}(X,Y) = \max_{f, g \in \mathcal{F}} \operatorname{corr}( \langle L_X,f \rangle, \langle L_Y,g \rangle) </math>

where the functions <math>f,g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}</math> range over <math>\mathcal{F}</math> and

: <math> \operatorname{corr}( \langle L_X,f \rangle, \langle L_Y,g \rangle) :=  \frac{\operatorname{cov}(f(X), g(Y)) }{\operatorname{var}(f(X))^{1/2} \operatorname{var}(g(Y))^{1/2} } </math>

for fixed <math>f,g \in \mathcal{F}</math>.<ref name = "Bach Jordan JMLR 2003" /> Note that the reproducing property implies that <math>f(x) = \langle L_x, f \rangle </math> for fixed <math>x \in \mathbb{R}</math> and <math>f \in \mathcal{F}</math>.<ref name = "Saitoh">{{cite book |last=Saitoh |first=Saburou | title=Theory of Reproducing Kernels and Its Applications |publisher=Longman |year=1988|isbn = 978-0582035645}}</ref> It follows then that the <math>\mathcal{F}</math>-correlation between two  [[Independence (probability theory)|independent random variables]] is zero.

This notion of <math>\mathcal{F}</math>-correlations is used for defining ''contrast'' functions that are optimized in the Kernel ICA algorithm. Specifically, if <math>\mathbf{X} := (x_{ij}) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}</math> is a [[Whitening transformation#Whitening a data matrix|prewhitened data matrix]], that is, the sample mean of each column is zero and the sample covariance of the rows is the <math>m \times m</math> dimensional [[identity matrix]], Kernel ICA estimates a <math>m \times m</math> dimensional orthogonal matrix <math>\mathbf{A}</math> so as to minimize finite-sample <math>\mathcal{F}</math>-correlations between the columns of <math>\mathbf{S} := \mathbf{X} \mathbf{A}^{\prime}</math>.
